idiom_name: extension functions toDto() / toDomain() next to the data classes; kotlinx.serialization for the wire shape
implementation_notes: Kotlin's idiom is one extension function per direction - `fun User.toDto() = UserDto(id = id, name = fullName)` and `fun UserDto.toDomain() = User(id = id, fullName = name, admin = isAdmin ?: false)` - which keeps the mapper out of both types while still reading as a member call at the boundary; data classes add `copy()` and destructuring inside the mapper body. kotlinx.serialization's `@Serializable` and `@SerialName` own only the wire representation - they rename and encode, they do not translate field meaning - so keep domain types free of `@Serializable` and put the serializable faces in the DTO layer. Choose a mapper class only when the same conversion must be configured or swapped at runtime (several API versions); otherwise top-level extension functions replace the classic mapper object entirely.
code_sketch:
// mapper/UserMappers.kt: one file owns both directions
fun User.toDto(): UserDto = UserDto(id = id, name = fullName, isAdmin = admin)

fun UserDto.toDomain(): User =
    User(id = id, fullName = name, admin = isAdmin ?: false)   // absent -> default
pitfalls: Extension functions are resolved statically and must be imported: a mapper in another module is invisible until imported, and scope-local extensions silently shadow same-named ones.
`copy()` is shallow - nested collections and mutable DTO fields stay shared between the domain object and the DTO, so mutating one changes the other.
Platform types from Java interop leak nullability into the mapper; declare DTO fields nullable and decide defaults in the mapper rather than relying on `!!` at the call site.
Inline/value classes and unsigned types in a DTO need explicit conversion; auto-generated `equals`/`toString` can hide a wrong mapping in tests that compare whole objects.
